title: Mortgage Rates Jump Back to 7.28%: What 17 Basis Points Cost
summary: Freddie Mac's 30-year average rose to 7.28% on November 19, ending a four-week slide. On a $400,000 loan the payment rises about $46 a month from last week and $271 from a year ago, and a buyer with a fixed $2,700 budget can borrow about $6,750 less.
description:
The four-week fall in US mortgage rates is over. Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey put the average 30-year fixed rate at 7.28% for the week to November 19, up from 7.11% a week earlier. A year ago the same survey stood at 6.26%. The move of 0.17 percentage points, or 17 basis points, wiped out more than the previous two weekly declines combined.

Freddie Mac's chief economist Sam Khater used the release to remind borrowers that comparing several quotes can save thousands over the life of a loan. That advice matters more when the weekly average swings this much, because the gap between lenders is often larger than the weekly move.

This PolicyRix Team analysis turns the new rate into dollars and checks it against other rate surveys.

What 7.28% means for a monthly payment

We used a $400,000 loan over 30 years and counted principal and interest only, before property tax, insurance or mortgage insurance.

At 7.11%, the monthly payment is about $2,691. At 7.28%, it is about $2,737. That is an increase of roughly $46 a month, or about $552 a year. Compared with a year ago at 6.26%, when the payment would have been about $2,465, the difference is about $271 a month.

Over the full 30 years, total interest at 7.28% comes to about $585,300, against about $568,700 at 7.11%. One week's move adds roughly $16,600 of lifetime interest if the borrower never refinances or prepays.

What it does to buying power

Another way to see the change is to fix the budget. A buyer who can afford $2,700 a month for principal and interest could borrow about $401,400 at 7.11%. At 7.28%, the same payment supports about $394,600, a drop of roughly $6,750 in one week. At last year's 6.26%, it would have supported about $438,100.

If a lender caps housing costs at 28% of gross income, the income needed for the $400,000 loan's principal and interest alone rises from about $115,300 at 7.11% to about $117,300 at 7.28%. Taxes and insurance push the real figure higher.

Other surveys point the same way

Freddie Mac's average is based on applications submitted through its Loan Product Advisor system, so it lags the daily market. Daily and lender surveys published in the same week sat higher. Bankrate's November 18 lender survey showed a 30-year average of 7.42%, up from 7.24% a week earlier. Mortgage News Daily's index was near 7.5% in mid-November. Fortune's daily table, built on Mortgage Research Center data, showed about 7.30% on November 19.

The spread between these series, about a fifth of a percentage point, is itself a reason to shop around. On our $400,000 example, 7.28% against 7.50% is worth about $60 a month.

What it means for refinancing

Homeowners who took loans at 7.5% or higher in 2023 and 2024 still have a case to refinance when rates dip, but the window narrowed this week. Our refinance break-even calculator shows how many months of savings it takes to recover closing costs. A higher new rate means smaller monthly savings and a longer break-even, so each week's move changes the answer.

What the data cannot tell us

Weekly averages describe a typical borrower with strong credit and a sizeable down payment. Rates quoted to a buyer with a lower score, a smaller deposit or a jumbo loan can be well above the survey. The numbers also cannot tell us where rates go next: the move followed higher Treasury yields, and those respond to inflation data and Federal Reserve expectations that change week to week. Finally, our payment figures leave out property taxes and homeowners insurance, which in many states have risen faster than principal and interest.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of Freddie Mac PMMS (November 19, 2026), Bankrate and Fortune rate tables
key_points: Freddie Mac's 30-year average rose to 7.28% for the week to November 19, from 7.11%, ending a four-week decline.
On a $400,000 loan, principal and interest rise about $46 a month from last week and $271 from a year ago.
A fixed $2,700 monthly budget now supports about $394,600 of borrowing, about $6,750 less than a week earlier.
Bankrate's lender survey showed 7.42% and daily indexes sat near 7.3% to 7.5%, so quotes vary widely.
Higher rates lengthen the break-even period for anyone considering a refinance.
why_it_matters: Buyers and refinancers make decisions on small rate moves. Turning the weekly average into dollars shows how much one week can change a budget, and why comparing quotes matters.

title: Reinsurance Costs Fell a Third. Why Home Insurance Bills Didn't
summary: Property catastrophe reinsurance rates fell about 12% and 16% at the two big 2026 renewals, and brokers expect at least 10% more on January 1. Compounded, that is about a third off in a year. US home premiums still rose 4% to 5% over the same period.
description:
Insurers buy their own insurance, called reinsurance, to protect themselves against big disasters. That cover has become much cheaper. Investment bank KBW expects property catastrophe excess-of-loss rates to fall by at least 10% at the January 1, 2027 renewals, after cuts of about 12% at January 2026 and 16% at the Florida-focused June 2026 renewals. Fitch reported that loss-free US property programmes saw cuts of up to 25% at mid-year.

Homeowners have not seen anything like that. This PolicyRix Team analysis compares the two trends and explains the gap.

How much cheaper reinsurance has become

If we compound the three renewals, a programme that cost 100 at the end of 2025 would cost about 88 after January 2026, about 74 after June, and about 66.5 after a further 10% cut in January 2027. That is a fall of roughly a third in about a year, on our arithmetic. Moody's said property catastrophe prices had already fallen more than 20% in the 18 months to mid-2026. RenaissanceRe told analysts in October that its own catastrophe book had seen mid-teens rate reductions so far in 2026.

The reason is supply. Gallagher Re says reinsurers enter the January renewals with record capital. Catastrophe bond issuance hit a first-half record of $17.3 billion, according to AM Best. And losses have been light: Gallagher Re estimates global insured natural catastrophe losses at $92 billion in the first nine months of 2026, 29% below the 10-year average and the lowest since 2019, with six straight quarters without a single $10 billion event.

What homeowners paid

Over a similar period, US home premiums kept rising, just more slowly. Insurify measured a 12% rise in 2025 and 2.2% in the first half of 2026, and projects 4% for the full year, taking its average from $2,948 to $3,057. NerdWallet's analysis of quoted rates found premiums up 4.6% from the first quarter of 2025 to the first quarter of 2026 and 24% since 2023.

Compounding Insurify's figures, a household paying 100 at the start of 2025 would pay about 116.5 by the end of 2026, on our calculation. Reinsurance has moved down by about a third while the retail price moved up by about a sixth.

Why the savings do not flow straight through

Reinsurance is only one part of a home insurance premium. The rest pays for everyday claims, such as burst pipes, hail and theft, plus repair costs, staff, commissions and taxes. Severe convective storms, the hail and wind events that drive many of those claims, caused at least $43 billion of US insured losses in the first nine months, Gallagher Re says, the fourth year in a row above $40 billion. Reinsurance rarely pays for those, because each storm is too small to reach the reinsurance threshold.

Prices also lag. Home insurance rates in most states need regulatory filings and approval, and insurers price for the future, not last quarter. After several years of losses, many insurers are rebuilding margins. The Insurance Information Institute and Milliman found homeowners insurers paid just 49 cents in claims for every premium dollar in the first half of 2026, their best first half in more than a decade, which shows that profits have recovered.

What it means for a homeowner

Cheaper reinsurance and strong profits should, in time, slow rate increases and bring more insurers back into hard markets. Shoppers in states where insurers had pulled back may see more choice at renewal. The best lever today is still to compare quotes and check deductibles, which our percentage deductible guide explains.

What the data cannot tell us

We do not know the share of an average US home premium that goes to reinsurance; it varies widely by insurer and state, and is far higher for coastal Florida carriers than for inland ones. Renewal price indices also describe typical programmes, not every insurer. And one major hurricane or earthquake before January could change the outlook quickly.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of KBW, Fitch, Moody's, Gallagher Re, Insurify, NerdWallet and Triple-I/Milliman data
image_alt: Shingled roof of a suburban house (illustrative)
key_points: KBW expects property catastrophe reinsurance rates to fall at least 10% on January 1, 2027, after cuts of about 12% and 16% in 2026.
Compounded, that takes reinsurance costs down by about a third in a year, on our arithmetic.
Insurify's figures imply US home premiums rose about 16.5% across 2025 and 2026 combined.
Hail and wind storms, which reinsurance rarely covers, caused at least $43 billion of US insured losses in nine months.
Homeowners insurers paid 49 cents in claims per premium dollar in the first half of 2026, their best result in over a decade.
why_it_matters: Homeowners hear that the insurance market is softening but still face higher bills. Knowing what reinsurance covers, and what it does not, explains the gap and what could change it.

title: UK Ombudsman Sides With Customers in Half of Claim Delay Disputes
summary: The first joint FOS and FCA report finds about 66,000 of 214,800 insurance complaints over five years were about delays, admin or service. Half of delay cases went the customer's way, against 34% across all insurance complaints, and 61% for travel.
description:
If your insurance claim stalls, the evidence now says you have a decent chance of winning a complaint about it. The Financial Ombudsman Service and the Financial Conduct Authority published their first joint thematic report on insurance claims on November 19, covering home, motor, travel and pet cover over the five years from April 2021 to March 2026.

This PolicyRix Team analysis looks at what the numbers say and what a policyholder can do with them.

The scale of the problem

Around 66,000 of roughly 214,800 insurance complaints the ombudsman handled over the period were about claim delays, administration and customer service. That is about 31% of the total, or roughly 13,200 a year on our arithmetic.

The ombudsman upheld 34% of all insurance complaints in the customer's favour. For claim delay complaints the rate was 50%, above average in every year reviewed. By product, Insurance Business reported uphold rates of 61% for travel, 53% for home across about 10,200 delay cases, 52% for pet and 46% for motor. Motor generated the most administration and service investigations, more than 13,000.

Put simply, a customer complaining about a delay was about 1.5 times as likely to win as the average insurance complainant, on our calculation from those two rates.

What the industry says

The Association of British Insurers said its members handled more than 25 million motor, home, travel and pet claims between 2021 and 2025, and that fewer than 1% led to an ombudsman complaint. Both things can be true: most claims go smoothly, but when a complaint reaches the ombudsman, the insurer often cannot show it handled the claim promptly. The FCA said 79% of people who claim are satisfied.

What the regulators want

The report does not create new rules. It explains how firms should meet existing ones, mainly the requirement to handle claims promptly and fairly and the Consumer Duty. The FCA asks insurers to keep claims moving, give clear and timely updates, and take responsibility when loss adjusters, repairers or other third parties working for them cause problems. Future reviews will look at management information on claim times, rejection rates and outcomes for vulnerable customers, who featured in about a quarter of complaints resolved in 2025/26.

Since the Which? super-complaint in 2025, the FCA has opened six insurance Consumer Duty investigations, three involving possible poor claims handling and fair value in home and travel cover. It says more than £200 million has been secured for motor customers whose cars were written off or stolen, and it will publish a progress update by the end of 2026. Further joint reports are planned.

What to do if your claim stalls

First, complain to the insurer in writing and keep a record of every call and email, including dates. Insurers have up to eight weeks to give a final response. If you are unhappy with it, or eight weeks pass, you can take the complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service for free. Mention specific delays and how they affected you; the ombudsman can award compensation for distress and inconvenience as well as the claim itself. If a repairer or loss adjuster is causing the hold-up, the insurer is still responsible.

What the data cannot tell us

Uphold rates only cover complaints that reached the ombudsman, which is a small and self-selected group. They do not show how many delayed customers gave up, or how long the average claim takes. The five-year totals also mix years with very different weather and repair backlogs, so they cannot tell us whether claim handling is improving now.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of the FOS and FCA joint thematic report (November 19, 2026), FCA, Insurance Business and Insurance Times
key_points: About 66,000 of 214,800 UK insurance complaints over five years, around 31%, concerned delays, admin or service.
The ombudsman upheld 50% of claim delay complaints, against 34% for insurance complaints overall.
Travel delay complaints had the highest uphold rate at 61%, followed by home at 53%, pet at 52% and motor at 46%.
The report adds no new rules but sets out what regulators will check, including oversight of repairers and loss adjusters.
Customers can go to the ombudsman free of charge after a final response or eight weeks.
why_it_matters: Claim delays are among the most common reasons people fall out with their insurer. The figures show complaints about delays often succeed, which tells policyholders when escalating is worth it.

title: Japan's Core Inflation Hits 2.2%, Keeping a December Rate Rise Alive
summary: Japan's core consumer prices rose 2.2% in October, the highest this year and above the Bank of Japan's 2% target for a second month. Markets see a rise to 1.5% on December 18 as likely, which would still leave the policy rate about 0.7 points below inflation.
description:
Japan's inflation is back above the central bank's target, and that keeps a December interest rate rise on the table. Core consumer prices, which exclude fresh food, rose 2.2% in October from a year earlier, up from 2.1% in September, according to data released on November 20. That was the highest reading of 2026 and the second month above the Bank of Japan's 2% target, though slightly below the 2.3% economists polled by Reuters had expected.

What changed

CNBC reported that the rise was driven by higher energy costs as government energy subsidies expired, with knock-on effects on other prices. A narrower measure that also strips out energy, often called core-core, slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%. Analysts said that easing partly reflected base effects from a year earlier rather than a clear cooling in underlying prices.

The national figure followed Tokyo data released in late October, which showed core prices in the capital up 2.6%. Tokyo numbers usually lead the national series by about three weeks.

Headline inflation, which includes fresh food, is watched less closely by the central bank because weather can move vegetable and fish prices sharply from month to month. The core measure is the one the Bank of Japan uses for its target, which is why the 2.2% reading drew so much attention from traders and economists.

What it means for interest rates

The Bank of Japan held its policy rate at 1.25% on October 30. Its next meeting ends on December 18, and many economists expect a rise to 1.5%. LSEG data cited in market reports put the probability of a quarter-point rise at about 72% after the release. Reuters noted the October figure strengthened the case even though the economy unexpectedly shrank in the third quarter. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda has also told parliament the bank is mindful of the weak yen, which has traded near 160 to the dollar and makes imports more expensive.

On our arithmetic, the gap between the policy rate and core inflation, a rough measure of the real policy rate, is about minus 0.95 percentage points today. A rise to 1.5% would narrow it to about minus 0.7 points. Policy would still be loose by that yardstick, which is why markets expect the bank to keep raising rates gradually.

What it means for households

For savers, higher short-term rates usually feed through to ordinary deposit rates at Japanese banks, though the pass-through is slower and smaller than the policy move. With prices rising 2.2% a year, money in a deposit paying well below that still loses buying power each year. Our guide to real returns shows how to work out what a savings rate is worth after inflation.

For borrowers, most Japanese home loans are variable-rate and many are linked to banks' short-term prime rates, which tend to follow the policy rate. A quarter-point rise on a 30 million yen variable loan would add roughly 75,000 yen a year in interest before any payment rules smooth the change, on our calculation. Many Japanese variable loans limit how often and how much payments can rise, so the full effect may arrive gradually.

For insurers, especially life insurers holding large amounts of Japanese government bonds, higher yields improve returns on new investments but can reduce the market value of existing holdings.

What happens next

The Bank of Japan will publish its December decision on December 18. Before then, Tokyo's November inflation data, due at the end of the month, will give an early read on whether price pressures are building or fading.
source_name: Statistics Bureau of Japan via CNBC, Reuters and investingLive
key_points: Japan's core CPI, excluding fresh food, rose 2.2% in October from 2.1% in September, below the 2.3% forecast.
Core inflation has been above the Bank of Japan's 2% target for two months running.
Markets put about a 72% chance on a rise from 1.25% to 1.5% at the December 18 meeting.
Even after a rise, the policy rate would sit about 0.7 points below core inflation, on our arithmetic.
Variable-rate borrowers and savers would feel any move gradually through bank prime and deposit rates.
why_it_matters: Japanese interest rates affect household mortgages, savings returns and the investment results of life insurers, and the yen's value moves global markets.

title: Canada Inflation Holds at 3.1%: What It Means for Rates and Savers
summary: Canada's annual inflation held at 3.1% in October, with energy up 21.8% while core measures stayed near 2%. The Bank of Canada's 2.5% rate is below headline inflation but above core, which helps explain why economists see a hold as possible on December 9.
description:
Canada's inflation rate did not move in October, and the details point in two directions at once. Statistics Canada reported on November 16 that the consumer price index rose 3.1% from a year earlier, the same as in September and slightly below the 3.2% economists had expected. Prices rose 0.2% from the previous month.

What drove the number

Energy did most of the work. Energy prices were up 21.8% from a year earlier, partly because gasoline prices fell sharply in October 2025, which makes this year's comparison look large. In month-to-month terms, gasoline actually fell 2.5% in October. Excluding energy, inflation eased to 2.0% from 2.1%.

Grocery prices sped up to 2.0% after four months of slower growth, and clothing jumped 3.4% in the month, the biggest monthly rise since 2019, which Statistics Canada linked to higher shipping costs. Cheaper cellphone plans and slower rent growth pulled the other way.

The Bank of Canada's preferred core measures were calm. CPI-median was 2.0% and CPI-trim 1.8%, so their average, as Desjardins calculated, fell to 1.9% from 2.0%.

Where that leaves interest rates

The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 2.5% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, saying it wanted to stop high energy prices spreading to other goods and services. Governor Tiff Macklem said further increases could be needed but the bank would proceed carefully, one meeting at a time.

On our arithmetic, the policy rate is about 0.6 points below headline inflation but about 0.6 points above the average core measure. That split helps explain the debate. If the bank looks at headline prices, policy still looks loose. If it looks at core, it already looks slightly tight. The next decision is on December 9, and November's inflation figures will not be published until December 14, after the meeting.

What it means for borrowers

Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit in Canada track banks' prime rates, which move with the policy rate. The October increase added about 0.25 points to those rates. On a C$500,000 variable-rate balance, that is roughly C$1,250 a year in extra interest, or about C$104 a month, before any change in amortisation, on our calculation. Borrowers with fixed payments may see more of each payment going to interest rather than to paying down the loan.

Fixed mortgage rates depend more on bond yields than on the policy rate, so they can move before or after the Bank of Canada acts.

What it means for savers

A savings account or GIC paying less than 3.1% is losing buying power on the headline measure. Measured against the 2% core rate, the picture is less bleak. Savers comparing GICs should look at the after-tax, after-inflation return, not the headline rate. Our real return guide walks through that calculation, and our compound interest calculator can show how the gap adds up over several years.

What happens next

Markets will watch the December 9 decision and the bank's language about energy. If energy prices fall back, the headline rate could drop quickly, because energy has been the main reason inflation sits above 3%. If energy stays high and begins to push up the price of groceries, clothing and services, the core measures would rise too, and the case for another increase would grow. For households, the practical step is the same either way: check whether a variable-rate loan still fits the budget at a rate half a point higher, and compare savings rates against inflation before locking money away.
source_name: Statistics Canada via The Canadian Press, Desjardins and Trading Economics; Bank of Canada
key_points: Canada's CPI rose 3.1% from a year earlier in October, unchanged from September and below the 3.2% forecast.
Energy prices were up 21.8% on the year, but excluding energy inflation eased to 2.0%.
The Bank of Canada's core measures averaged 1.9%, down from 2.0%.
At 2.5%, the policy rate sits about 0.6 points below headline inflation and about 0.6 points above core.
The next rate decision is December 9, before November inflation data are released on December 14.
why_it_matters: Canadian mortgage holders, savers and anyone with a line of credit are affected by how the Bank of Canada reads inflation. The split between headline and core makes the December decision harder to call.

title: IRDAI Pushes Insurers to Clear Old Disputes in November
summary: IRDAI has made November a Grievance Resolution Month, asking insurers to settle long-pending disputes and comply quickly with ombudsman awards. About 2.21 lakh insurance cases were pending in consumer commissions and courts in March, 72% of them for over a year.
description:
India's insurance regulator wants insurers to clear their backlog of old disputes, and it has given them a month to make progress. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India announced on October 29 that November 2026 would be a Grievance Resolution Month, focused on long-pending policyholder grievances and disputes.

What IRDAI asked for

According to the regulator's circular, as summarised by TeamLease RegTech, insurers should review all pending matters and prioritise the oldest, settle cases amicably where that is legally and factually sustainable, comply promptly with Insurance Ombudsman awards, and speed up grievances pending before other forums. They are also asked to strengthen litigation management and find the recurring causes of complaints so the same problems stop coming back.

IRDAI said the goal is fair, meaningful and lasting resolution, not just higher disposal numbers. The Life Insurance Council, the General Insurance Council and the Council for Insurance Ombudsmen are supporting the drive, and outreach programmes are planned with special attention to Tier-II and Tier-III cities.

The size of the backlog

The figures behind the push are large. About 2.21 lakh insurance cases, or roughly 221,000, were pending before consumer commissions and courts as of March 31, 2026. About 72.49% of them had been pending for more than a year, which on our arithmetic means roughly 160,000 cases at least a year old. Separately, around 11 lakh cases were reported pending before Motor Accident Claims Tribunals, where most disputes concern third-party motor claims.

The chairman's message

IRDAI chairman Ajay Seth returned to the theme on November 19 in a keynote at the CII-DFS Financing Summit in Mumbai. He said insurance is a promise, and the test of any reform is whether that promise is kept when the customer needs it most. He argued that the real value of a policy lies in what the policyholder receives when a claim arises, not in what was promised at the time of sale.

Seth has made faster and fairer claims a recurring message. At a Business Standard event in October he said the sector must grow 1.5 to 2 times faster than the economy, with faster claim settlement, more transparency and lower distribution costs. He has also said effective insurance coverage in India could double from about 15% to 30% within five years.

What it means for policyholders

If you have a dispute with an insurer that has dragged on, this month is a good time to follow up. Write to the insurer's grievance officer, quote your complaint number and ask for a resolution date. If you are not satisfied within 30 days, or the insurer rejects the complaint, you can approach the Insurance Ombudsman, which handles disputes up to a set value without a fee. If the ombudsman has already ruled in your favour and the insurer has not paid, mention the regulator's instruction to comply promptly with awards. IRDAI's Bima Bharosa portal can also be used to register and track complaints.

What remains unclear

The circular does not set numerical targets or say how results will be reported. The test will be whether the share of cases older than a year falls when the next annual figures are published, and whether repeat complaints about the same issues, such as health claim deductions, become less common. Policyholders who are still waiting should keep copies of every letter, claim form and hospital bill, because a well-documented case is far easier for an insurer or ombudsman to resolve quickly.
source_name: IRDAI circular of October 29, 2026 via TeamLease RegTech; CII-DFS Financing Summit remarks via NewKerala; Business Standard
key_points: IRDAI declared November 2026 a Grievance Resolution Month to clear long-pending policyholder disputes.
About 2.21 lakh insurance cases were pending in consumer commissions and courts on March 31, 2026, 72.49% for over a year.
Insurers are asked to settle sustainable cases amicably and comply promptly with ombudsman awards.
Chairman Ajay Seth said on November 19 that reform should be judged by whether claims are honoured when needed.
Policyholders can escalate to the Insurance Ombudsman if the insurer does not resolve a complaint within 30 days.
why_it_matters: Long disputes leave policyholders waiting years for money they may be owed. A regulator-backed push gives customers with old cases a reason to follow up now.
